extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in entertainment news and controversies (Netflix, comedians, public responses)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing public and institutional criteria used to judge comedy that targets or references atrocities, marginalized groups, or other sensitive topics, as reflected in media coverage and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: No mocking of racist genocide / atrocities
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mocking racist genocide has no place in comedy or a decent society.” (quoted from MP Zarah Sultana / Nadia Whittome)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements from politicians condemn jokes that make light of genocides; such material is labeled 'grotesque' and politicians urged Netflix to remove it. The page presents this as a categorical moral standard: genocide and similar mass atrocities are not appropriate subjects for mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making light of victims' experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: “Hundreds of thousands of Roma and Sinti people suffered prejudice, slave labor, sterilization and mass murder simply because of their identity — these are not experiences for mockery.” (Holocaust Memorial Day Trust CEO Olivia Marks‑Woldman)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes specific harms (prejudice, slave labor, sterilization, mass murder) and asserts that those lived experiences should not be treated as comedic material. Used as a normative boundary for acceptable comedic targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the content fuel prejudice or defile memory?
rubrics_metrics.description: The Auschwitz Memorial: 'It’s sad to hear words that can fuel prejudice, hurt people & defile memory of their tragedy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates jokes by their downstream effects on public prejudice and on the collective memory of victims; content that risks normalizing or encouraging prejudice is condemned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educational framing as a defense — plausible or not?
rubrics_metrics.description: Jimmy Carr's claim that the joke has 'an educational quality' because it raises awareness that Nazis also killed Roma, homosexuals, disabled people and Jehovah’s Witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some comedians frame controversial jokes as raising awareness or teaching historical facts; the article presents this claim alongside criticisms, implying evaluators should weigh whether educational intent justifies the harm or trivialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of trigger/warning prefaces for sensitive material
rubrics_metrics.description: The special begins with: 'Trigger warning: Tonight’s show contains jokes about terrible things...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creators may provide content warnings for shows containing jokes about traumatic subjects; the article notes the warning but also cites Carr's follow-up minimization ('These are just jokes. They're not terrible things.'), raising questions about whether warnings are sufficient mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between joking about harm and enacting harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Carr: 'There’s a huge difference between doing a joke about a rape ... And doing a rape … I fucking hope.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoked as a defense of transgressive comedy (claiming a moral/ontological difference between joking and committing). The page contrasts this defense with backlash, indicating critics may reject that distinction as a sufficient justification in cases of severe harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reaction as an indicator of normalisation or harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Observers noted 'gales of laughter' followed Carr’s remarks, which the Holocaust Memorial Day Trust said was 'horrifying.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether an audience laughs (and the scale of the reaction) is presented as evidence of normalization or complicity; evaluators may use audience response to judge acceptability and social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform responsibility and regulatory accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: U.K. culture secretary Nadine Dorries suggested new laws to hold streamers like Netflix accountable and to bring streaming platforms under Ofcom regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond individual responsibility, the article records calls for platform-level remedies (content removal, regulation, legislation) — a criterion for evaluation includes whether platforms should permit, moderate, or remove controversial material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calls for content removal as an appropriate remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple MPs and campaigners 'call on @netflix to remove this grotesque material.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removal is presented as a demanded or possible response; evaluators and stakeholders consider deletion from platforms as an appropriate corrective when content crosses perceived moral/ethical lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/educational duty vs. trivialisation in public discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Carr argues that many people don't know Roma were also targeted because 'it's not really taught in our schools'; he frames repeating the topic as a form of remembrance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises a criterion weighing whether public discourse (including comedy) responsibly informs public understanding of history or instead trivializes it; evaluators should assess whether the net effect is increased awareness or trivialization and harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent and institutional consequences for controversial material
rubrics_metrics.description: References to prior controversies (Whoopi Goldberg suspended for Holocaust comments; Dave Chappelle controversy leading to employee walkouts) as context for responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past cases and their institutional outcomes (suspension, employee protest, public backlash) serve as precedent when judging and responding to similar incidents; they inform expectations for consequences and acceptable responses.
